Suppose we ask an agent to refactor an entire backend. The work may cover configuration loading, authentication, and tests. One agent can process those areas sequentially, but it takes longer and earlier details gradually leave its context.

authentication, and tests, preserve the existing interfaces,
and make sure the tests pass.

The Agent is fixing a bug. It reads many files to trace the call chain, and every tool call and result stays in the parent's `messages[]`. Once the call chain is understood, most of those intermediate details are no longer needed, but they still occupy context.

---

## The Solution

![Subagent Overview](images/subagent-overview.en.svg)

Calling `task` synchronously runs a nested agent loop with a fresh `messages[]`. When that loop finishes, its final text becomes the tool result in the parent conversation.

This is message isolation, not process or filesystem isolation. Parent and subagent run in the same Python process and share `WORKDIR`, so writes and commands still affect the same workspace. The subagent has the five base tools but no `task`, and its tool calls use the same permission and lifecycle hooks as the parent.

---

# Chapter s13 Tutorial: Agent Teams — Teaching Your Assistant to Work as a Team

## What this chapter teaches

This chapter belongs to a course that rebuilds, piece by piece, how an AI coding assistant works on the inside. Earlier chapters built a single agent loop, file and shell tools, hooks, permissions, and (in chapter s10) a shared task system. Chapter s13 adds the team layer: one main agent called the Lead, plus helper agents called teammates that can work at the same time, talk to each other, and share work safely.

If you have never worked with AI agents before, here is the one-sentence summary: instead of one assistant doing every job alone, chapter s13 shows how to let that assistant propose a small team, split a big job into tasks on a shared board, and let persistent teammates pick up and finish those tasks in parallel — all while you, the user, stay in control.

By the end of this tutorial you will understand: when a team is useful, how teammates get started, how they communicate without confusing each other, how they find work on their own, why tasks can point at separate working directories (worktrees), and how stopping a teammate or approving a plan is made strict and traceable.

## The problem: one pair of hands is not enough

Imagine you ask an assistant to refactor an entire sample backend. The job touches configuration loading, authentication, and tests. One agent can do these one after another, but it is slow, and agents have a limited working memory (a context window). While it works on tests, details about configuration quietly fall out of that memory, so quality can drift.

Humans solve this with a team: one person handles configuration, another handles authentication, another writes tests. Chapter s13 gives the assistant the same option. Importantly, you do not have to design the team. You just say what you want:

"Refactor this backend. Clean up configuration loading, authentication, and tests. Preserve the existing interfaces and make sure the tests pass."
